newsitem.title: INDIA: Hindu-Moslem clashes cloud key Indian state polls.
newsitem.headline: Hindu-Moslem clashes cloud key Indian state polls.

text.p: Indian security forces tightened their vigil in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh on Sunday where Hindu-Moslem clashes revived old tensions ahead of crucial state assembly polls.
Tens of thousands of paramilitary troops have been deployed to guard the three-phase elections, starting on Monday in the violence-prone state.
With 140 million people, the sprawling state is more populous than Japan or Pakistan.

Police imposed an around-the-clock curfew in the Moslem- majority old quarter of Lucknow, the state capital once ruled by the colourful Shi'ite Moslem nawabs of Oudh, now the main base of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Officials said police pulled the body of an unidentified man from a gutter on Saturday after Hindu and Moslem groups clashed on Thursday and Friday over the erection of a Hindu idol in old Lucknow.
Scores of people were injured in the clashes.
It was not clear if the man was killed in those clashes.

Politicians said the polls, involving 90 million eligible voters, would test Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ability to ride out a challenge by the BJP, India's main opposition group which is campaigning for mid-term parliamentary polls.
"It is inevitable now that mid-term polls for parliament will be held sooner than later," BJP President Lal Krishna Advani told reporters in Lucknow on Sunday.
"There are too many contradictions in this government."

The BJP derives its major strength from Uttar Pradesh where its campaign to build a Hindu temple at the site of a 16th century mosque catapulted it to power in several north Indian states and made it the main opposition in parliament in 1991.

Militant supporters of the BJP demolished the Babri mosque in Ayodhya, 200 km (120 miles) east of Lucknow, in December 1992, triggering nationwide Hindu-Moslem riots in which more than 3,000 people died.
Hindu militants claim two more mosques in the western Uttar Pradesh city of Mathura and in Varanasi on the state's eastern flank, saying they stand on sites of ancient Hindu temples.
While the BJP is playing down the issue in its campaign, the government, taking no chances, has staggered the polls over three days to cover the three disputed sites on different days.

The assembly polls will see Deve Gowda's fractious United Front alliance take on the Congress party, which supports his minority government in Delhi, and the BJP in a triangular fight for the state's 425-member Vidhan Sabha, or lower house.
Uttar Pradesh sends 85 deputies to the 545-member federal parliament, where the BJP is the biggest single party.

Analysts say the state, once a bastion of the Congress party which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, could boost a recent trend of coalition politics that helped Deve Gowda form a minority government in June.
On the other hand, a poll by the Times of India on Sunday predicted a possible victory for the BJP, saying the Hindu nationalists could get betwen 205 to 215 seats.
Advani said his party hoped to get 236 assembly seats.

Deve Gowda formed a minority government in June after Rao promised to support him following inconclusive general elections, and remains beholden to the Congress to survive the BJP's unceasing challenge in parliament.
The polls in northern Uttar Pradesh will test that equation, analysts said.
